analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums due to preexisting conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill, which barred health-status discrimination by insurers, died in two House subcommittees in 1995 and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Health Insurance Equity Act of 1995 would have stopped health insurers and employer health plans from denying coverage, limiting benefits, or charging higher premiums because of a person's health history or past claims. It would have capped preexisting-condition exclusions at six months, required insurers to renew policies, and set up state enforcement with federal penalties as a backstop. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who change or lose jobs and fear losing coverage, people with preexisting conditions such as diabetes or cancer histories, newborns and pregnant women, and small employers with fewer than 50 employees buying coverage. A person switching jobs could count prior coverage against a preexisting-condition exclusion instead of starting over, and no one could be priced or refused based on medical history.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with preexisting conditions and job-changers

how_it_helps.text: Bars insurers and group health plans from denying, limiting, or conditioning coverage, or varying premiums, based on health status, claims experience, receipt of health care, or medical history.

Caps preexisting-condition exclusions at six months, lets months of prior continuous coverage count against the exclusion, and prohibits any exclusion for newborns covered at birth or conditions related to pregnancy.

Requires insurers to renew individual and small-employer coverage except for narrow reasons like nonpayment or fraud; an insurer leaving the market must give 180 days' notice and is barred from reentering that market for five years.

Makes each state set up an enforcement program, authorizes federal grants to pay for it, and lets the federal government impose civil money penalties of $150 per day per affected person on noncomplying insurers if a state's enforcement is inadequate; the Labor Department enforces the rules for employer plans under ERISA.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans, which would have to cover sicker enrollees at standard rates and could no longer screen out costly customers; those costs would be spread across premiums. Taxpayers would fund federal grants to states for enforcement. Insurers that wanted out of a market would bear the cost of the five-year reentry ban.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: Insurers could still exclude a preexisting condition for up to six months, and could offer to waive the exclusion only by charging the person a higher premium.
Premiums could still vary based on age, sex, and where a person lives, so older people and women could still face higher prices.

An insurer could stop enrolling any new individuals or small employers in an area altogether if it demonstrated to the state insurance commissioner that its financial or provider capacity would be impaired.

Enforcement depended first on state insurance commissioners; federal penalties would apply only after the Secretary of Health and Human Services found a state's program inadequate and the state failed to correct it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections would have been genuinely valuable for people with medical histories and for anyone changing jobs, which in the 1990s meant many workers stayed in jobs they hated just to keep insurance. The bill was a moderate design: it preserved a six-month exclusion window, allowed age, sex, and geography rating, and leaned on state enforcement, so it regulated insurers at the edges rather than restructuring the market. The main cost — insurers bearing the claims of sicker enrollees — is the point of the bill and would largely have been spread through premiums.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House subcommittees from early 1995 onward and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James A. Hayes introduced the bill on January 9, 1995, joined by one Republican cosponsor, Rep. Jim McCrery.
The Speaker referred it to two committees — Commerce, and Economic and Educational Opportunities — splitting jurisdiction over its insurance and employer-plan provisions.
On January 25, 1995 it was referred to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, and on February 21, 1995 to the Health and Environment Subcommittee.
No further action of any kind is recorded through the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers were better off because the bill died: they avoided federal limits on health-status underwriting and a guaranteed-renewal mandate. Workers with preexisting conditions who changed or lost jobs in those years gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Rep. James A. Hayes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its health-status nondiscrimination standards on January 9, 1995.

for.name: Rep. Jim McCrery
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the bill was referred on January 9, 1995; it went to subcommittee and never returned for a markup or vote.

against.name: House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral; its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee received the bill on January 25, 1995 and nothing further happened.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded support was a Democratic sponsor with a single Republican cosponsor, both from Louisiana.

industries.note: The bill would have ended health-status underwriting — the practice of charging more or refusing people with medical histories — and required guaranteed renewal, forcing insurers to spread the cost of sicker enrollees across all customers. Insurers that wanted to exit a market could, but with 180 days' notice and a five-year reentry ban.

Plans covering employees would have faced the same nondiscrimination, preexisting-condition, and enrollment rules, enforced by the Labor Department. Larger employers already covered workers regardless of health, so the burden fell mostly on how plans handled new hires and job-changers.

HMOs would have been bound by the same rules, but the bill explicitly allowed HMO-style preexisting-condition exclusions so long as they followed the new limits, and permitted managed care plans to drop people who moved out of the service area.
States would have gained a federal mandate and grant money to build enforcement programs, with federal civil penalties as a backstop against weak enforcement.
